title: Civil War: Israel Against Benjamin
summary: All Israel assembles at Mizpah, hears the Levite's account, and vows to punish Gibeah. When Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty men, the tribes go to war against their brothers. Israel loses two battles despite inquiring of the LORD, then weeps, fasts, and sacrifices at Bethel; on the third day an ambush succeeds, and Benjamin is nearly annihilated, with only six hundred men escaping to the rock of Rimmon.
story: Chapter 19 ended with the dismembered body sent throughout Israel and a call to take counsel. Chapter 20 shows the nation's response. For the first time in the book, all Israel acts as one, but against one of its own tribes. The unity that the judges could never achieve against foreign enemies is found only in civil war. The story echoes earlier moments in Israel's history: the assembly recalls the covenant gatherings of Joshua, the question of who shall go up first recalls 1:1, and the ambush recalls the taking of Ai (Joshua 8). But the enemy is now Benjamin, and the victory is a catastrophe. The chapter leads directly into chapter 21, where Israel must deal with the near extinction of a tribe.
historical:
Mizpah in Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem, was a traditional place of assembly, later used by Samuel (1 Samuel 7:5-6; 10:17). Bethel, a little further north, was the location of the ark of the covenant at this time (20:27), though the tabernacle is elsewhere associated with Shiloh. The mention of Phinehas son of Eleazar, Aaron's grandson, who was already active in the wilderness (Numbers 25:7-13), places these events early in the period of the judges.

The numbers in the chapter are very large: 400,000 Israelite soldiers, 26,700 Benjamites, and tens of thousands of casualties. As with other large numbers in the historical books, some scholars suggest that the Hebrew word usually translated thousand ('eleph) sometimes means a military unit or clan contingent, which would reduce the figures considerably; others take them at face value or see them as expressing the scale of the disaster. The chapter's own totals also vary slightly (25,100 in 20:35, 25,000 in 20:46), a common feature of ancient narrative that gives a detailed count in one place and a round number in another.
cultural:
Israel's tribal confederation had no central government, but it did have mechanisms for collective action: assemblies before the LORD, oaths, and a shared sense of covenant obligation. The demand that Benjamin hand over the guilty men reflects Deuteronomy's principle of purging evil from Israel (Deuteronomy 13:5; 17:7; 22:21-22), which the text quotes in 20:13. Benjamin's refusal put tribal loyalty above covenant justice.

Casting lots and inquiring of the LORD, probably through the high priest's Urim and Thummim, were the normal means of seeking God's direction in war. Weeping, fasting, and offering burnt offerings and peace offerings expressed repentance and dependence before God. The Benjamite slingers were famous: 1 Chronicles 12:2 describes Benjamite warriors who could use both hands with a sling or bow. The irony that left-handers came from Benjamin, whose name means son of the right hand, is noted by many readers; the left-handed Ehud was also a Benjamite (3:15).
literary: The battle account is built on a threefold pattern. Three times Israel inquires of the LORD, each time with more humility: first asking only who should go first (20:18), then weeping and asking whether to go up again (20:23), and finally weeping, fasting, and offering sacrifices before asking whether to go or stop (20:26-28). Only on the third inquiry does the LORD promise victory. The final battle is told twice, first in summary (20:29-36a) and then in detail (20:36b-48), a technique used elsewhere in Hebrew narrative. The repeated phrase as one man (20:1, 8, 11) emphasizes Israel's unity, but it is a unity in vengeance. The Levite's speech (20:4-7) leaves out his own part in the concubine's death, a silence the reader who knows chapter 19 cannot miss.

outline.t: Israel assembles at Mizpah and hears the Levite
The tribes vow to punish Gibeah
Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty and prepares for war
The first two battles: Israel defeated
Weeping, fasting, and sacrifice at Bethel
The third battle and the ambush
Gibeah burned and Benjamin nearly destroyed

doctrines.note: The crime at Gibeah demands justice, and the LORD finally gives Israel victory. But the scale of the destruction shows judgment carried out by a people who were themselves compromised, with terrible cost to all.

Israel's successive inquiries show a movement from self-confidence to humility. Only after weeping, fasting, and sacrifice does the LORD promise success. The chapter suggests that those who execute judgment must themselves come before God in repentance.
Benjamin's refusal to hand over the guilty shows how tribal loyalty can shield evil. The civil war that follows is a consequence of sin that spreads from individuals to a whole community.

words.note: Nevalah, disgraceful act or outrage, used by the Levite in 20:6 and by the assembly in 20:10. It names a crime against the covenant order itself. The whole nation agrees that what happened at Gibeah was such an outrage, which is why they act together.
Zimmah, lewdness or wickedness, often used for sexual sin or shameful plans. The Levite pairs it with nevalah in 20:6. The two words together emphasize the depth of the evil done at Gibeah.

Ba'ar, to burn, and in this form to purge or remove. The phrase purge Israel of this evil in 20:13 echoes Deuteronomy's commands to remove evil from the community. Israel sees its war as fulfilling that duty, though the result goes far beyond the punishment of the guilty men.

Qahal, assembly, used in 20:2 of the gathering of God's people. The word describes Israel gathered before the LORD for covenant purposes. The Greek translation often rendered it ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church, which makes this failing assembly a sobering picture.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is thematic. Israel sought to purge evil from its midst, but the effort to do so consumed a whole tribe and left the nation grieving. The problem the chapter exposes, that God's people cannot purge evil without being overwhelmed by it, is taken up in the New Testament's account of Christ bearing the judgment for sin himself (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). The church is also called to deal with sin among its members (1 Corinthians 5:13, which quotes the same Deuteronomic phrase about purging evil), but through discipline aimed at repentance and restoration, not the destruction of the offender's family and town. The chapter's picture of an assembly united in vengeance stands against the New Testament picture of an assembly united in Christ.

hard.q: If the LORD told Israel to go up to battle, why were they defeated twice?
hard.a: The text records that the LORD answered Israel's inquiries, yet Israel lost forty thousand men in the first two battles. Interpreters offer several explanations. Some note that Israel's first inquiry asked only who should go first, not whether to fight at all, and that Israel went into battle confident in its own strength; the defeats humbled them until, on the third inquiry, they came with weeping, fasting, and sacrifice. Others suggest the defeats were a judgment on Israel as well as Benjamin, since the whole nation had drifted into the idolatry and moral chaos shown in the epilogue, and the war was a disaster for all the tribes. Still others emphasize that God's command to go up did not guarantee immediate victory, and that the story shows the cost of a war among brothers. The text does not explain directly; it lets the pattern of the inquiries and the suffering speak.

questions: Israel acted as one man only when fighting against one of its own tribes. What does it take for communities to find unity for good rather than for vengeance?
Benjamin protected guilty men because they were its own. Where do loyalty to a group and commitment to justice come into conflict?
Israel came to the LORD with more humility each time. Why might God's people need to be humbled even when they are pursuing a just cause?
